by_task.when: ARIZONA is allowable and the asset fits an Arizona category.
by_task.procedure: Treat statutory dollar limits as caps, not eligibility thresholds: include § 33-1125(8) for a motor vehicle and § 33-1125(10) for a firearm even when value exceeds the limit. Include § 33-1101(A), not subsection (B), as the homestead exemption alternative. Confirm the statutory category before applying its cap.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel; § 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings, and subsection (B) is a one-homestead limitation rather than a separate asset exemption. Non-ring jewelry does not qualify under either § 33-1125(1) or § 33-1125(4).

by_task.when: FEDERAL is an allowable namespace and the asset is property of the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate every applicable specific paragraph, then independently include 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5), which can protect any property. A dollar ceiling limits protection rather than eligibility. Thus a vehicle remains eligible under § 522(d)(2) above its cap, jewelry uses § 522(d)(4), and § 522(d)(5) remains an additional alternative even when a specific paragraph applies.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(3) for an unlisted category such as a firearm or jewelry, do not omit a specific paragraph because value exceeds its ceiling, and do not repeat a citation.

by_task.when: FEDERAL is allowable and an eligible asset-exemption pair needs a claim value.
by_task.procedure: Compute each alternative independently. Use the lesser of asset value and $4,450 under § 522(d)(2), $700 per item under § 522(d)(3), or $1,875 under § 522(d)(4). Under § 522(d)(5), use the lesser of asset value and $1,475 plus the unused § 522(d)(1) amount, up to $13,950; apply § 522 separately to each debtor in a joint case.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not reject an otherwise eligible asset merely because its value exceeds a ceiling, and do not treat § 522(d)(3) as covering firearms or other unlisted categories.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and the property is held for personal rather than business use.
by_task.procedure: Evaluate 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) independently as the any-other-property alternative, including when apparel, a motor vehicle, or a prescribed health aid also has a specific exemption. Section (a) covers necessary wearing apparel, (c) covers a motor vehicle, and (e) covers professionally prescribed health aids. A value above a limit does not eliminate either applicable alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use § 12-1001(d) for ordinary household property; it requires implements, professional books, or tools of the debtor's trade. Do not classify jewelry or a watch as necessary wearing apparel under subsection (a), and do not omit subsection (b) merely because a specific subsection applies.

by_task.when: ILLINOIS is allowable and an eligible personal-use asset-exemption pair needs valuation.
by_task.procedure: Compute overlapping alternatives separately. For § 12-1001(b), use the lesser of value and $4,000 for one debtor, or $8,000 for jointly owned property of two debtors. For § 12-1001(c), use the lesser of value and $2,400; this vehicle limit is not doubled. Thus a jointly owned vehicle may have both an $8,000 subsection (b) alternative and a separate $2,400 subsection (c) alternative. Sections (a) and (e) have no stated dollar ceiling in the supplied text, so use the asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not assign the $8,000 joint wildcard amount to subsection (c), replace the $2,400 vehicle limit with a wildcard limit, omit subsection (b) because a specific subsection applies, or apply these personal-property exemptions to business-use property.

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent general personal-property alternative even when a more specific Oregon exemption also applies, including for a vehicle or professionally prescribed health aid.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the general alternative for the specific category exemption, apply it to real property, or classify wearing apparel as household goods under § 18.345(1)(f).

by_task.when: OREGON is allowable and § 18.345(1)(p) applies to personal property.
by_task.procedure: Report the § 18.345(1)(p) alternative independently at the lesser of the asset value and $400, while retaining every applicable specific Oregon alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit the alternative because the asset exceeds $400; the limit caps the amount rather than eligibility.

by_task.when: PENNSYLVANIA is allowable and the debtor owns the property.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent general monetary exemption for the property, whether or not a specific federal or Pennsylvania exemption also applies and whether or not the property's value exceeds the monetary limit.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not invent a specific Pennsylvania category, use a specific category belonging to a different kind of property, or treat a firearm as wearing apparel under § 8124(a)(1).

by_task.when: PENNSYLVANIA is allowable and § 8123 is evaluated.
by_task.procedure: Claim the lesser of the asset value and $300 under § 8123; for married debtors, each spouse is entitled to the exemption, allowing up to $600 on jointly owned property.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because another exemption applies, and do not exceed the applicable single- or married-debtor limit.
